title: U.S. Bancorp, *checked every morning*
summary: The biggest bank run from Minneapolis: how it makes money, how it compares with its rivals, and how much of it is really local.

blocks.body: I took U.S. Bancorp apart using SEC filings, bank regulators’ data, and research databases licensed through the University of Minnesota. This page has the main findings and a chart that updates itself every morning. The [full report](/us-bancorp-report/) has every number and where it came from.

items.title: Its lead over rival banks has mostly gone
items.text: In 2005 it earned about 21 points more on its equity than its typical rival. By 2024 the bank itself was slightly behind. The parent company is still a little ahead, but mainly because it holds less equity, not because it earns more on its assets.

items.title: Shareholders did worse than at rival banks
items.text: Counting dividends, its stock returned 61%. The typical rival returned 178%. It came last of ten.

items.title: Fees are what still set it apart
items.text: Fees were 40% of its revenue, against 27% for its typical rival. It also runs the biggest corporate trust business of any U.S. bank.

items.title: Its cheap deposits shrank
items.text: Deposits that pay no interest fell from 29% of the total to 16%. Only one of its ten rivals was lower. That made its money more expensive when interest rates went up.

items.title: It was hit harder in 2022 and 2023
items.text: Its capital cushion was below its typical rival’s almost every year from 2015 to 2025. When rates jumped, its bond losses were the second worst of 11, and its stock fell further than its rivals’ in the March 2023 bank scare. Bond investors stayed calmer than stock investors. Its capital moved above the typical rival’s only in 2026.

items.title: Most of its Twin Cities deposits are probably not local
items.text: On paper it holds 41% of the area’s deposits. But 85% of that sits in two downtown offices that likely hold business from across the country. Leave those two out and its share is about 15%, the same as in 1994.

items.title: It lends far less to local small businesses than it used to
items.text: Its share of small-business lending in the Twin Cities fell from 36% to 9%. Over the same years its local deposit share stayed near 15%.

items.title: The Twin Cities share of its jobs has not been shrinking
items.text: About 17% of its U.S. employees work here, close to the 2010 share. It rose to 20% by 2020 and dropped when the Union Bank deal added California staff. These counts are estimates built from online job profiles.

items.title: The books look clean
items.text: No restatements and no material weaknesses in any annual report. The money it sets aside for bad loans looks about average for its peers.

blocks.heading: How the chart stays current
blocks.body:
Every morning, a small program runs on GitHub, not on my computer. It checks the FDIC, the SEC, the Federal Reserve, the Federal Register and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau for anything new about the bank.

The word at the top of the chart is the result. **No change** means nothing new. **Review** means new quarterly numbers came out. **Revisit** means something serious happened, like a regulator’s order or a big swing in the numbers, and I need to reread part of the report.

items.title: Public data first
items.text: Filings, regulator data and court records, plus stock, bond, analyst and workforce data licensed through the University of Minnesota. Each file is logged with where it came from and when.

items.title: Every section checked twice
items.text: A second, separate review redid some of the math in each section and argued against its conclusions. The report uses the corrected versions.

items.title: Built with AI
items.text: AI models did the collecting, the math and the first drafts, under my direction. Every number traces back to a public source or a piece of code, so you can check it.

blocks.heading: What I still can’t answer
blocks.body: Some questions need records that aren’t public: what those two downtown offices really hold, how the Union Bank purchase has done on its own, and what workers are actually paid. The last one needs Census data that takes an application and about a year to get.
